title: GPU Programming Model Basics
summary: The host/device split and the thread/block/grid hierarchy every GPU kernel is organized around.

slides.markdown:
GPU programs run on two processors at once: the **host** (the CPU) and the **device** (the GPU). The host runs your normal program, allocates memory on the device, copies data over, and tells the device *what* to run and with how many threads — but the host never executes the parallel work itself.

The device just waits for instructions: it has no operating system, no independent control flow of its own. This split is why a GPU program always looks like "CPU code that occasionally launches a burst of GPU work," never a program that runs entirely on the GPU end to end.

A **kernel** is the function the host launches onto the device — but you write it *once*, from the point of view of a single thread, and the runtime executes that same function body across potentially millions of threads simultaneously.

Inside the kernel, each thread reads its own unique index and uses it to decide which piece of data it's responsible for. There's no loop over "all elements" in the code itself — the loop is implicit, expressed by how many threads you launch, not by iteration.

Threads aren't launched as one flat pool — they're organized into a **thread → block → grid** hierarchy. A **block** is a group of threads that can cooperate (share memory, synchronize); a **grid** is the full set of blocks launched for one kernel call.

This structure isn't bureaucracy — it maps directly onto hardware: a block is scheduled onto one physical execution unit as a whole, which is exactly why threads *within* a block can share fast on-chip memory ([gpu-memory-hierarchy](gpu-memory-hierarchy)) while threads in different blocks generally can't cooperate directly at all.

A grid of blocks, each holding many threads, maps down onto the GPU's physical SIMT execution units — the runtime schedules whole blocks onto available hardware as capacity frees up.

![A grid made of multiple blocks, each block containing many threads, mapped onto physical GPU execution units](assets/grid-block-thread-hierarchy.svg)

A kernel launch might request far more blocks than the chip can run at once — the GPU simply queues the rest and starts them as earlier blocks finish, so the same kernel scales across GPUs with very different core counts without any code change.

assets.alt: A grid made of multiple blocks, each block containing many threads, mapped onto physical GPU execution units

slides.markdown:
GPU kernels are naturally **map-style**: the same pure function applied independently to every element, with no shared mutable state between iterations.

| | GPU kernel (map-style) | General CPU code |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | One function, N independent invocations | Arbitrary control flow, shared state |
| Data dependence | None between elements (ideally) | Frequent — loops carry state forward |
| Fits well | Elementwise math, filters, reductions | Parsers, trees, stateful simulations |

Code with sequential dependencies between iterations — this element's result depends on the last one's — doesn't map onto this model well; forcing it onto a GPU usually means restructuring the algorithm, not just "porting" it.

slides.subTitle: Getting data to the device isn't free
slides.markdown:
Every byte a kernel operates on that starts out in host (CPU) memory has to physically cross the PCIe bus to reach device memory before the kernel can touch it, and results have to cross back to be usable by the rest of the program. That transfer runs at PCIe bandwidth — tens of GB/s — dramatically slower than the GPU's own on-device memory bandwidth (hundreds of GB/s to over a terabyte/s on datacenter parts, [GPU Memory Hierarchy](gpu-memory-hierarchy)).

For a kernel that does very little compute per byte transferred, this **host-to-device and device-to-host copy time can dwarf the actual kernel execution time** — a classic beginner mistake is measuring only kernel runtime and concluding a GPU port was a huge win, while ignoring that the copies surrounding it ate most of the wall-clock benefit. Real GPU pipelines minimize this by keeping data resident on the device across many kernel launches instead of shuttling it back and forth per call.

slides.sectionTitle: Synchronization: within a block, across the grid, and across host/device
slides.subTitle: Three different guarantees, easy to confuse
slides.markdown:
`__syncthreads()` (a barrier) only guarantees ordering **within one block** — every thread in that block reaches the barrier before any of them proceeds past it. It says nothing about threads in a *different* block; blocks can execute in any order, even simultaneously across different hardware, so there is no built-in way for one block to wait on another mid-kernel.

At the host/device boundary, a kernel launch is **asynchronous by default**: the host call returns immediately, and the CPU keeps running while the GPU works in the background. Explicit synchronization (`cudaDeviceSynchronize()` or waiting on a stream/event) is required before the host can safely read results the kernel produced. Forgetting this is a classic race-condition bug: reading device output on the host before the kernel has actually finished, silently getting stale or partial data instead of a crash.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: when the copy costs more than the compute
slides.subTitle: A PCIe-bound kernel launch
slides.markdown:
Transferring 1GB to the device, running a kernel, then transferring 1GB back. PCIe 4.0 x16 gives roughly 25 GB/s achievable; the kernel itself takes 2ms to compute.

```
host-to-device copy = 1GB / 25GB/s = 40ms
kernel compute       = 2ms
device-to-host copy  = 1GB / 25GB/s = 40ms

total wall time = 40 + 2 + 40 = 82ms
compute's share of total time = 2 / 82 ~= 2.4%
```

The kernel itself is nearly free next to the copies surrounding it — this workload gained almost nothing from the GPU port unless the same device-resident data can be reused across many more kernel launches, amortizing that 80ms of copy cost across far more than 2ms of compute. This is exactly why real GPU pipelines batch work and keep data resident on-device rather than launching one kernel per small transfer.
